JUDGMENT Learned Additional Government Advocate accepts notice for respondents 1 to 4.
This intra-court appeal is filed under Section 4 of the Karnataka High Courts Act challenging the order dated 30.05.2022, passed in W.P.No.22818/2011 by the learned Single Judge.

2. Brief facts leading rise to filing of this appeal are as under:
Appellant's father was the owner of lands bearing Sy.No.211/1, 211/2, 219 and 222 situated at Bogadi Village, Mysuru Taluk & District.

The appellant's father had declared his holdings under Section 7 of the Urban Land (Ceiling & Regulation) Act,
1976 ('the Act of 1976' for short), in respect of the above said lands and other lands before the competent authority.
The competent authority passed an order under Section 9 of the Act of 1976.
As per the order, the appellant was found to be holding 17806.72 sq.meters in Sy.No.219 in excess of the ceiling limit.
Respondent No.4 has not paid any compensation as contemplated under Section 11 of the Act of 1976 in lieu of acquisition of the land.
On 27.12.1988, the land in question was notified for acquisition by respondent No.2.

2 proceedings in respect of land in question.

sentences.text: The respondent No.2 requested respondent No.1 to release the land in question from the alleged acquisition with some other properties of the appellant's brother in the same village.
Respondent No.3 agreed to purchase the land bearing Sy.No.219 and other lands of appellant and his brothers.
Respondent No.3 paid the sale consideration amount to an extent of 3 acres 4 guntas out of 4 acres 16 guntas in Sy.No.219.
Respondent No.4 highhandedly took possession of land in Sy.No.219 measuring 1 acre 12 guntas and removed the standing trees on the land in question.
The appellant filed a writ petition questioning the illegal acts of the respondents and also final statement dated 12.11.1985 vide Annexure-A and order dated 14.10.1989, vide Annexure-C.
The learned Single Judge after hearing the parties, dismissed the writ petition on the ground of delay and laches.
The appellant, aggrieved by the order passed by the learned Single Judge, has filed this writ appeal.

3. Heard Sri.R.S.Ravi, learned senior counsel for the appellant and learned Additional Government Advocate for respondents 1 and 4.
4.
Learned senior counsel for the appellant submits that the physical possession of the land in question was not taken by the respondents.

He submits that the competent authority vide Annexure-C has specifically directed Mysuru Urban Development Authority to take possession of land which is in excess of ceiling limit and no proceedings are initiated for taking possession of land.
He further submits that the learned Single Judge failed to consider that the appellant has not been paid any compensation by the respondents for acquiring 1 acre 12 guntas in Sy.No.219.
He submits that the learned Single Judge has committed an error in dismissing the writ petition on the ground of delay and laches.
The impugned order is arbitrary and erroneous.
Hence on these grounds, he prays to allow the writ appeal.
5. Learned Additional Government Advocate supports the impugned order.

6. Perused the records and considered the submissions of the learned counsel for the parties.
7.
Appellant's father was the owner of lands bearing Sy.No.211/1, 211/2, 219 and 222 situated at Bogadi Village, Mysuru Taluk & District.
The appellant's father had declared his holdings under Section 7 of the Urban Land (Ceiling & Regulation) Act, 1976, in respect of the above said lands and other lands before the competent authority.
The competent authority passed an order under Section 9 of the Act of 1976.
As per the order, the appellant was found to be holding 17806.72 sq.meters in Sy.No.219 in excess of the ceiling limit.
The proceedings under the Act of 1976 were initiated vide order dated 12.11.1985.
The writ petition was filed in the year 2011.
Thus there is an inordinate delay of 26 years in filing the writ petition.
The petitioner has not explained the delay in filing the writ petition at a belated stage.

The Hon'ble Apex Court in the case of CHENNAI METROPOLITAN WATER SUPPLY AND SEWERAGE BOARD & OTHERS VS. T.T. MURALI BABU, has held as under at paragraphs 16 and 17:

sentences.text: Thus, the doctrine of delay and laches should not be lightly brushed aside.
A writ Court is required to weigh the explanation offered and the acceptability of the same.
The Court should bear in mind that it is exercising an extraordinary and equitable jurisdiction.

As a constitutional Court it has a duty to protect the rights of the citizens but simultaneously it is to keep itself alive to the primary principle that when an aggrieved person, without adequate reason, approaches the Court at his own leisure or pleasure, the Court would be under legal obligation to scrutinize whether the lis at a belated stage should be entertained or not.
Be it noted, delay comes in the way of equity.
In certain circumstances delay and laches may not be fatal but in most circumstances inordinate delay would only invite disaster for the litigant who knocks at the doors of the Court.

Delay reflects inactivity and inaction on the part of a litigant - a litigant who has forgotten the basic norms, namely, "procrastination is the greatest thief of time" and second, law does not permit one to sleep and rise like a phoenix.
Delay does bring in hazard and causes injury to the lis.

In the case at hand,
though there has been four years' delay in approaching the Court, yet the writ Court chose not to address the same.
It is the duty of the Court to scrutinize whether such enormous delay is to be ignored without any justification.

That apart, in the present case, such belated approach gains more significance as the respondent-employee being absolutely careless to his duty and nurturing a lackadaisical attitude to the responsibility had remained unauthorisedly absent on the pretext of some kind of ill health.
We repeat at the cost of repetition that remaining innocuously oblivious to such delay does not foster the cause of justice.

On the contrary, it brings in injustice,
for it is likely to affect others.
Such delay may have impact on others' ripened rights and may unnecessarily drag others into litigation which in acceptable realm of probability, may have been treated to have attained finality.
A Court is not expected to give indulgence to such indolent persons - who compete with 'Kumbhakarna' or for that matter 'Rip Van Winkle'.
In our considered opinion, such delay does not deserve any indulgence and on the said ground alone the writ Court should have thrown the petition overboard at the very threshold.

17. Having dealt with the doctrine of delay and laches, we shall presently proceed to deal with the doctrine of proportionality which has been taken recourse to by the High Court regard being had to the obtaining factual matrix.
We think it appropriate to refer to some of the authorities which have been placed reliance upon by the High Court."
(emphasis supplied)
8. Further, the appellant has also filed a suit in O.S.No.271/2011 against the Government and the said suit came to be dismissed vide judgment and decree dated 20.07.2015.
In the said suit, the trial Court has recorded a finding that the appellant is not in possession of the property in question.
The said judgment and decree passed by the trial Court has attained finality.
The learned senior counsel submits that the finding recorded by the trial Court that possession of land was not taken by Government, cannot be accepted for the reasons stated above.

The learned Single Judge was Sri G Puttaiah vs The State Of Karnataka on 10 February, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/153646907/
4 justified in dismissing the writ petition on the ground of delay and laches.

sentences.text: We do not find any grounds to interfere with the impugned order.
Accordingly, we decline to interfere with the impugned order.

Hence we proceed to pass the following:
ORDER
The writ appeal is dismissed.
In view of disposal of the writ appeal, pending IAs., if any, do not survive for consideration and are accordingly disposed of.
